## Why GRPO suits long reasoning

Appendix A.3 gives reasons beyond saving memory. A value model must predict the final reward from a *partial* response. That is hard when only a final outcome reward exists, and harder for long chains of thought, where early text may later be revised or contradicted through reflection.

The KL treatment differs too. In GRPO an estimator of the KL divergence is added directly to the loss. In PPO a per-token KL penalty is added as a dense reward, so the cumulative penalty may implicitly penalize length and discourage longer responses. Since training runs thousands of steps and the policy can drift far from the starting point, the authors periodically refresh the reference policy.

A fair caveat from the paper's own experiment (a smaller model on the MATH task): PPO with the default GAE $\lambda=0.95$ was clearly worse than GRPO, but after tuning $\lambda$ to 1.0 it came close. So GRPO is presented as the more *practical* choice, not as strictly superior.
